**Diary of a Cave-Dwelling Fish, Near the Lizard**

**Date: A Moonlit Night in Late Summer**

Another strange day in the deep, shadowy world of our cave. The great rock walls tremble often now, for the two-legged creatures come more frequently in their hollow wooden shell. Today they rowed far inside, their boat scraping against the ledges where I hide. One of them made a terrible noise—a sudden, sharp crack like a thunderclap under the sea. The sound echoed and echoed, shaking the water around me. I darted behind a thick frond of seaweed until the ringing stopped. I have heard this before; they call it a “pistol.” It is their way of playing in the dark.

But the worst is what happens after sunset. I do not venture near the sandy shore when the bright round light floats in the sky—they call it “moon.” For then the other fish, the slender silvery ones that burrow in the wet sand, become easy prey. I have watched from a cautious distance: the giants stand ankle-deep, with crooked iron spears, and strike quickly. One of them, the one they call John Curgenven, is especially swift. He never misses. His boat often passes our cave, and I have seen his stout arms and honest face many times. He seems kind to his own kind, but to us he is a hunter.

Tonight the moon is full, and I heard the merriment of the fishermen on the beach after their catch. They lit a fire and cooked my cousins. I stayed deep within the cave, listening to the waves and the occasional pistol shot from a passing boat. The Lizard Lights glow far away, but they do not warm me. I am a fish of the cave—safe, for now, in the gloom. But I know that when the moon rises again, the spears will come once more.

**Diary Entry – Kynance Cove, Cornwall**

*September 12th, 18—*

What a day of wild beauty and caution! Kynance Cove is everything the guidebooks promised—and more. But the Devil’s Throat (some call it Hell’s Mouth) left the deepest impression on me.

We had heard of it before we came. The boatman warned us not to attempt it, and the kind clergyman we met on the sands spoke of it with a mixture of awe and dread. It is a gaping fissure in the rock, with a yawning cave beneath and a wide chasm that must be leaped. The jump, they say, is a good one, and if you miss your footing—well, you would be swallowed by the sea. I saw a young man and woman crawling like flies along the face of the rock toward that very place, while a distressed gentleman shouted at them to come down. “She’ll never manage it!” he cried. I confess I felt a cold shiver.

Legend clings to this spot like the sea-fog. Locals mutter of a devil’s mouth that once swallowed careless climbers, and the name alone is enough to make one think twice. Our clerical friend of this morning—a sensible man who admires bravery but despises foolhardiness—said he would never let his own daughters attempt it. They were content with the easier scramble up Asparagus Rock. Wise folk!

For my part, I am content to admire the Throat from a safe distance. The rocks here are like black teeth, and the waves boil around them with a hungry sound. It may be a fine sight for the daring, but I shall keep my limbs whole and my curiosity in check. Some legends are best left untested.

**Diary Entry of the Parrot**

**Day of My Passing**

I write this with my last breath, for my time in this bright world is done. I was born among the emerald trees of the East, a gift to my mistress from distant lands. She loved me dearly, and I her. In her home among the groves, I would call to the guileless birds and mimic the voices of men. My tongue was more skilled at talking than any other bird, and my mistress delighted in my prattle.

But I witnessed much trouble in that house. Her lover was often in distress, accused of casting eyes upon her handmaid, Cypassis. My mistress would watch him with suspicion, and he would plead and argue, though I could see his heart was true to her alone. Many a night I heard their quarrels, and I felt the sorrow in his sighs.

One day, my mistress bade me farewell. I knew not why, but I was sent away from the groves. Perhaps I was a reminder of a love that had grown weary. I was taken from her side, and though I called for her with my lisping notes, she did not come.

Then, I was snatched away by cruel hands. Envy stole me from the world, for I was the best of birds, and the best are always taken first. Now a small sepulchre covers my bones, and on a little stone is my inscription: "From this very tomb I may be judged to have been the favorite of my mistress."

I rest now, but my heart still longs for the groves and for her voice. Let the vulture live, and the kite, and the hateful crow—they may endure for ages. But I, who gave her laughter and words, am laid low. Farewell, my mistress. May you find peace, and may your lover know your heart at last.

Another morn, and I have not yet seen the mother of the swarthy Memnon rise with her rosy horses. They call me Dipsas – and rightly so, for I am ever athirst, never sober when dawn breaks. Yet what need have I of wine when the very elements obey my will? Let me record the secrets I possess, lest any fool think my power mere legend.

I know the magic arts and the charms of Ææa – those of Circe and Medea, whose names echo from Colchis. With my skill I turn the flowing stream back to its source; the waters themselves cannot resist my whispered words. I know what the herbs of the field can do, and what the thrums of the spinning-wheel accomplish when wound about with incantations. And that venomous exudation from the prurient mare – ah, its potency is beyond the ken of common men.

When I will it, the clouds overspread the sky; when I will it, the day brightens. I have beheld the stars dripping with blood, the moon empurpled with gore. They call me Dipsas, and rightly so—never does the rosy-fingered dawn catch me sober. The name fits like a second skin, for I drink as deeply of the vine as of the dark arts. Let the world think me a mere drunken crone; they little know the power that coils in these withered fingers.

This evening, I sat with the foolish girl—my mistress’s charge—and taught her the arts that open men’s purses and loosen their tongues. She is eager but crude; she has yet to learn that a glance, a pause, a feigned tear works more wonders than a hundred embraces. I showed her how to set her locks in proper order, to seem innocent while her eyes promise all. The memory of that accursed poet’s curses still rings in my ears—let him rage. His anger only feeds my fire.

But I digress. My true craft lies not in petty seductions but in the old, the deep, the forbidden. I am kin to Circe and Medea, the women of Ææa. I know the herbs that poison or heal, the thrums of the spinning-wheel that bind a man’s fate as surely as a thread binds a loom. I have seen the venomous exudation from a mare in heat—a subtle poison that drives the strongest warrior to madness. When I wish it, the clouds gather and blacken the sky; when I wish it, the sun blazes clear. I have beheld stars dripping with blood, and the moon’s face empurpled with gore—omens I have called forth for my own purposes.

They say I can fly, transformed into a strix, a shrieking bird of the night. Let them believe—or not. I have done so, and the taste of the air high above the rooftops is sweeter than any wine. And my eyes—ah, my double pupils—they strike fear into the boldest. A mere look can blight a harvest or curdle milk in the udder. The evil eye, they call it. I call it a gift.

Tonight, as I drank alone, I murmured a charm to turn back a nearby stream—to remind myself that even nature obeys me. The water stopped, trembled, then flowed upstream. I laughed. Let the poet curse me; let the lovers weep. I am Dipsas, and the world bends to my whispers.

**October 15th, 18—**

Dear Diary,

I hardly know where to begin. Today was the most terrible and wonderful day of my life. I am safe now, back in Aunt Katy’s warm kitchen, writing by the firelight. But let me set it down as it happened.

This morning, I was walking near the camp when Tom Ditamus—that mean, lazy man—caught me by the arm. He had an ugly gag in his other hand. He told me if I made a noise, he would put the bit in my mouth and tie the straps behind my head. I screamed once, but then I remembered Aunt Katy’s words: “Discretion is the better part of valor.” So I stopped. He shoved me into his covered wagon, between his dirty children, and gave the gag to his wife. He told her to put it on me if I made the slightest sound.

All day we drove south through thick fog. Ten miles they went with a lazy ox team. I sat quiet and thought. I knew I had to escape that very night, or I would never find my way home. I remembered Aunt Katy saying, “If there is a will, there is a way.” So I waited.

When night came, Tom and his family fell asleep by the bank of a creek. I crept away as light as a timid cat. I followed the Kentucky River, because I knew it would lead me to Port William. Sometimes the road left the river and went into the hills, but I stayed close to the water, even when I had to push through briars and dark woods. I had no lamp, only the stars.

Then I came to White’s Creek. The water was deep and dark. An owl hooted from the other side, and it seemed to say, “Come over, little gal.” I sat down and wept. But I remembered my own good sense. I traced the creek on the south side until I found a ford. Then I crossed and followed the creek back on the north side until I reached the big road. I pulled off my shoes and waded across.

After that, I ran as fast as I could. At dawn I saw the chimneys of Port William. My heart leaped! I hurried to Aunt Katy’s house. The door was not fastened. I crept in, and there she sat by the cold hearth, her face in her hands. She was asleep. I touched her head and whispered, “Aunt Katy.” She woke and held me close, and we cried together.

I told her everything—my capture by Tom Ditamus, my escape through the woods, the river, the creek, the owl. She said she understood it all. The Demitts wanted me taken away, but I am free now. I will never leave Aunt Katy again.

Yours faithfully,
Suza Fairfield

**Diary Entry – Young Simon**

*April 6, 1861*

I am writing this by the dim lamp in my hotel room in Chicago, though my hand trembles and my breath comes short. The physicians say I have but little time left, and the truth of it settles on me like a pall. Yet there are things I must set down, for my mind will not rest.

Cousin Cæsar is with me, as faithful as ever. He is the son of my father’s brother, though I knew little of that branch of the family until lately. He was raised by two sisters, “big-sis” and “little-sis,” poor washerwomen who gave him what they had. He told me once of a bubble on the suds that he imagined would turn into a loaf of bread—and “big-sis” gave him her last crust. That story haunts me. It speaks of a kindness I have rarely known.

My father—S. S. Simon—was a hard man, a keen financier who worked himself to death in the swamps. He left me a vast estate, but no family name to be proud of, and a body too weak to enjoy it. I remember little of him except his dying delirium. Through the night he cried out, “Take Roxie Daymon away.” Those words echoed in my ears when I first heard that name on the steamboat. I cannot explain it, but I feel a thread of fate pulling me toward her.

Roxie. She is beautiful, full of life, and has consented to marry me—a dying man. Why? I dare not question the good Angel’s silence. Perhaps she sees something in me that I cannot see. Perhaps she knows more of my father’s history than I do. Cousin Cæsar seems to know some part of it, though he keeps his counsel.

Now I lie here, my strength fading. The marriage is put off until I am better, but I know I will never stand alone again. I have made my will, leaving everything to Roxie. Cousin Cæsar will see to the rest. I only pray that whatever mystery binds us will be resolved—and that my dying father’s words will not prove a curse upon us all.

*Young Simon*

But I see also a *kanoon*, strung with lamb’s gut, three strings for each note, played with two little plectra bound to the fingers. That too is familiar. Our own *chang*—which some here mistake for a harp—is more like a dulcimer in truth, and I recall that the Arabs called it *junk* after they took it from us. Indeed, when the Arabs conquered Persia in the seventh century, they found our music and our instruments far superior to their own. They adopted them eagerly, and from that adoption, the whole system of Arabian music was shaped.

What strikes me most is the continuity. Here, in a glass case, lies a *santir* that could have been played in the courts of Ctesiphon, and beside it a *huayra-puhura* from Peru—eight pipes of talc, arranged in a scale that seems arbitrary to European ears. Yet both are born of the same human impulse: to stretch a string or to drill a tube and call it music. The museum’s collections show us that our Persian *santir* has cousins in every land, from the Egyptian harp to the Chinese *cheng*. Even the *free reed* of the harmonium, so popular here, came from China by way of a Russian organ builder who saw a *cheng* and took the idea.

I feel that we Persians, though our empire has crumbled, have left an indelible mark on the world’s music. The *santir* is not merely an instrument; it is a bridge between ages and peoples. I shall return tomorrow to sketch its proportions, for the illustration in the museum’s book—taken from a Persian painting—does not do justice to the way the light catches the wire strings.  

— *A.H., London*

**June 12th, 18—**

What a ridiculous, extraordinary, yet strangely delightful day it has been. I was in the garden this morning, watering the myrtle and trying to shake off the oppressive heat, when a most unexpected visitor arrived—not through the gate, but from the wall itself! I felt the color drain from my face. He meant my father, or perhaps my brother. They must have intercepted it. That explains his silence; it was never his doing.

I did not know whether to be furious with my family or relieved. But he stood there, looking so earnest and absurdly disheveled, that I found myself softening.
